Absent active concessions, positions harden and a trilateral package drifts further away.

gm_decisions.intent: Look, Mexico just accepted 75% regional value content plus a labor value floor. Canada either matches that package or we move forward without them—simple as that. And we're not softening on enforceable labor provisions; that's non-negotiable for us to sell this to Congress.
gm_decisions.ruling_narrative: The U.S. ultimatum forces a critical clarification moment, but the room fragments into parallel sub-debates (audit mechanisms, wage floors, dairy) before consensus can form. No single agent blocks outright, yet no coherent package emerges—the proposal is denied as premature until these interlocking questions resolve.

_reactions.canada_min: Okay, 75% RVC — we can live with that. But on labor enforcement: Mexico's saying their own courts do the work, we verify after. That's not enforcement, that's hoping. Before Canada locks in, I need clarity — is the *mechanism* for labor verification set in stone with the U.S., or can we talk about what "independent verification" actually means?
_reactions.mexico_neg: Canada, the labor mechanism is set with the U.S.—that's not on the table. But what *is* negotiable between us is how fast your plants come into the audit cycle and what the transition period looks like. You either shape that timeline with us now, or you're explaining to your auto sector why they're out of the deal. What's your real constraint here?
_reactions.us_congress: Canada, you said you need clarity on the mechanism — you've got it now. Real-time audits, Mexican courts enforce, U.S. suspends benefits if they slip. That's teeth. So what's your actual timeline constraint? If it's a 3-year phase-in for your plants, can you live with that, or is this about something else?
_reactions.auto_industry: Before Canada and the U.S. lock horns on audit structure—can we be clear on what "joint panel" means operationally? Does it mean U.S. inspectors *can't* audit Canadian plants solo, or just that there's a review process after? Because if it's the latter, my members need to know the audit cycle and cost upfront—we can't absorb surprises.
_reactions.labor_union: Hold on — audit panels and timelines don't matter if Mexico's still got no wage floor or independent union protection baked into the deal. You can audit all day; if there's nothing to enforce, Congress kills this. So before Canada and the U.S. lock in audit structures, what's the actual **Mexican wage commitment** and who certifies independent unions? That's what labor needs to see.
_reactions.dairy_ag: Canada, I hear the joint-panel concern, but let's be direct: if we solve the audit structure your way, what does Canada put on the table to move this deal forward? Because right now labor enforcement, sunset clauses, and auto RVC are all locked. Dairy's the one thing we haven't discussed—and frankly, that's where my government sees real value in a trilateral package.
_reactions.supply_chain_mfr: Before we nail down audit cycles and panels, I need to know: what's the actual Mexican wage floor baked into this deal, and how does Mexico certify independent unions? Because my members can absorb compliance cost and a 3-year phase-in, but not audit infrastructure for a deal that has no teeth on wages. That kills us in Congress anyway — so what's on the table with Mexico?

gm_decisions.intent: Alright, here's the move: Mexico puts a **minimum wage floor in writing**—indexed to their manufacturing average, independent union certification in the agreement itself—and we audit that quarterly, not hypothetically. Canada gets the same audit structure as Mexico, 3-year phase-in. In exchange, Canada opens dairy market access—real quota reductions, not gestures. That's a deal Congress can sell.
gm_decisions.ruling_narrative: USTR's package advances: Mexico commits to indexed minimum wage and quarterly audits; Canada opens dairy quotas on cheese/yogurt.

side_effects.reason: Major trilateral framework emerging with concrete commitments
Quarterly audits and indexed wage floor strengthen enforcement
Dairy concessions breach supply management principles
Concrete labor and dairy wins address Congressional concerns

_reactions.canada_min: Alright, I hear you—dairy's the ask. We'll open quota on select categories: cheese, yogurt, but not fluid milk or butter. Indexed phase-in, five years. That's real market access your Congress can defend, and it keeps supply management intact. But in exchange: Chapter 19 stays, and we lock the audit structure as-is—no reopening labor or auto rules once Mexico and I sign on.
_reactions.mexico_neg: Look, Chapter 19 is yours—that's not Mexico's problem. On dairy, Canada's offering cheese and yogurt on a five-year phase-in; that's what you've got to work with Congress on. But here's the real ask: commit to the audit structure *now*, or we're moving forward without you. What's your answer?
_reactions.us_congress: Here's what I need from you two: Canada puts a hard-floor commitment in writing — minimum annual quota for cheese at [X thousand metric tons] and yogurt at [Y], non-renegotiable for five years, then subject to review. Dairy_ag, that's your insurance against year-three shrinkage. Canada, that's how you keep supply management real and move this deal forward. What are those numbers?
_reactions.auto_industry: Seventy-five percent RVC is workable, but here's what I need locked down *today*: what's the labor-value-content floor—15%, 20%?—and does Mexico get a full 3-year phase-in from signature, or does it clock from entry-into-force? My members can absorb the compliance hit, but not moving targets. Give me the timeline in writing.
_reactions.labor_union: Dairy_ag, Canada's offering hard minimums on cheese and yogurt—non-renegotiable five-year floor. Does that number actually work for your members, or are we still short? Because if there's daylight here, we need to close it now—labor enforcement doesn't matter if the deal falls apart over dairy.
_reactions.dairy_ag: Hold on—Congress just asked for the numbers. What's the actual metric-ton floor you need on cheese and yogurt for your vote? Because my members won't say yes to a "hard floor" that doesn't have a number attached.
_reactions.supply_chain_mfr: USTR, before this package goes to Congress, what's the U.S. position on the sunset — automatic termination in five years, or a review mechanism that keeps the deal alive unless someone actively kills it? My members won't build new lines or lock in suppliers if they're planning for a deal that expires.

_reactions.canada_min: Look, 15% is a non-starter if Congress won't ratify. Here's what I'm putting on the table: Canada matches **18% labor-value content**, phased in over three years, *but* only if Mexico's wage floor and independent union certification are locked in the agreement text—not a side letter, not "we'll strengthen courts later." That's what my Parliament needs to defend this, and it's what your labor members need to see. Can we do that?
_reactions.mexico_neg: Canada, I hear the Parliament concern, but here's the reality: Mexico's wage floor and audits are locked in the agreement text—that's done. Union certification runs through Mexican labor law; we're not negotiating that away. You either sign onto this package today or you're out. What's your answer?
_reactions.us_congress: Mexico, I hear the sovereignty concern, but here's the reality: Congress won't ratify a deal where we audit wages but have no independent eyes on union certification. You don't have to change Mexican labor law—but you do have to let independent auditors *verify* that certification happened, as part of the quarterly audit cycle. That's not a trilateral panel, it's just confirmation. Can you live with that, or are we done?
_reactions.auto_industry: Hold on—Canada just moved to 18% labor value, USTR said 15%. Before my members commit to retooling, I need one number: is 18% the locked floor for all three countries, and does the three-year phase-in clock from signature or entry-into-force? Give me that in writing and we're good.
_reactions.labor_union: Mexico, I hear the sovereignty line—and 18% labor value with indexed wages gets us most of the way. But here's what my members need to hear from you *right now*: independent auditors verify union certification *as part of* the quarterly audit, and if the verification shows no independent union or wage violations, the U.S. can suspend trade benefits. That's not a panel rewriting your labor law—it's just confirming what happened. Yes or no, because Congress votes on ratification the minute we leave this room.
_reactions.dairy_ag: Canada, you moved on labor-value content and the audit structure—that's real. _reactions.supply_chain_mfr: USTR, you said review mechanism—does that mean the deal auto-renews unless all three vote to kill it, or does it sunset and we renegotiate from scratch in year five? My members won't lock in new supply contracts without knowing which one it is.
